validation.summary:
Both validated source traces establish public legacy read/CLI conversion -> main_text -> Story::blocks without a field-depth budget. N begin/separator pairs incur O(N²) Boolean visits; balanced closing controls and result text add scans. At depth 100000, roughly 300 KiB of balanced delimiters requires billions of Boolean examinations. The additional native read_document refusal path invokes legacy_doc::read to decide whether to print a DOC conversion hint, so refusal is not an early protection.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently verified Unencrypted DOC -> legacy_doc::read -> main_text -> Story::blocks -> fields.iter().any on each character; BEGIN pushes true, SEPARATOR changes top to false, END pops.
Assigned discovery-0010 Standard corroboration (source validation, not reducer verification): Parent read main_text control decoding and Story::blocks. Each0x13 pushes true;0x14 makes the newest entry false. Repeating this pair leaves all ancestors false and causes scans summing1+2+...+N; balanced0x15 closes also scan before popping. Physical CFB bounds do not constrain this later work.
Assigned discovery-0007 corroboration (preserved Standard static validation; no reducer verification): For [0x13,0x14] repeated N times followed by N 0x15 markers, the stack grows then shrinks while mostly/all false. Sum of traversed depths is quadratic; N=100000 uses 300000 physical text bytes and tens of billions of predicate checks.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified public read decodes piece-table text to StoryChar values and calls Story::blocks; compressed and UTF-16 decoders preserve field control characters. Each start/separator pair grows an all-false stack, so iter().any scans a progressively larger prefix. No field-depth cap intervenes in the inspected path.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed compressed text retains begin/separator/end codes 0x13/0x14/0x15. Repeated begin+separator pairs model nested fields in their result phase; every all-false prefix is rescanned before later input. Public legacy read invokes this function on the complete decoded story.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified the character loop and state transitions; no field-depth budget or cached active-code count exists. Early exit for a true outer code flag is avoided by opening each child after the enclosing separator. Closing the fields still produces a supported parser path; no recursion is required for this CPU attack.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Parent verified that nested field starts and separators can maintain a growing all-false stack; on that state fields.iter().any scans all active levels. Repetition yields cumulative quadratic work even without physical piece reuse. Unclosed nesting is accepted until input end. Public read/conversion and native refusal hints reach this loop.
Assigned discovery-0024 corroboration (supplied already-validated Standard assessment; no reducer verification): For n nested begin/separator pairs left in their result state, each separator and subsequent character scans an increasing all-false vector. Closing them later or supplying n result characters preserves quadratic comparisons. No text reuse or physical-offset violation is required.
Supplied discovery-0030 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Verified that legacy public read constructs Story and calls blocks on decoded main-text characters, and that CLI compound-file conversion reaches that API. For n begin/separator pairs the all-false scans cost 1+2+...+n; balanced end fields do not remove prior work.
Supplied discovery-0029 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): After N begin/separator pairs the stack contains N false entries. Processing successive pairs examines prefixes of length 0..N, totaling Theta(N^2) boolean checks; N closing field markers can also scan decreasing false prefixes. A single physical text piece is sufficient, so bounding repeated physical ranges does not remediate this separate complexity failure.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.
Endnote numStart/format also reaches the same shared formatter through number_endnote_refs; its generated-label budget must cover that route as well as list, page and agent/MCP read-view consumers.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified initial counter selection, render formatting and repeat arithmetic. A start of 4294967295 selects the double-dagger marker and requests 3,221,225,472 UTF-8 bytes. XML size and depth remain small; source byte limits cannot prevent the allocation.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): For n=2147483647, i=n-1=2147483646; i%4=2 selects the three-byte double dagger, and i/4+1=536870912 produces 1610612736 bytes before copies. List starts, startOverride, reader starts, endnote numStart and page pgNumType.start are parsed without a maximum. Both Numbering::render and the agent reader call the shared formatter. The native read_view adapter calls markdown::read (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:899-901).

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.
Endnote numStart/format also reaches the same shared formatter through number_endnote_refs; its generated-label budget must cover that route as well as list, page and agent/MCP read-view consumers.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: A shared formatter converts a bounded-width but numerically huge input into output proportional to its magnitude, without checking the resulting label length before String::repeat.

rootCause.summary:
List starts/startOverrides and section pgNumType starts retain full u32 values. Numbering::next_marker uses the authored first counter and substitutes format_num output; section_page_label independently dispatches its page counter through format_num. Chicago calls chicago_label, which computes i=n.saturating_sub(1) and MARKS[i%4].repeat(i/4+1) without a bound. Markdown list-label generation uses the same shared formatter. Counter saturation prevents overflow but retains enormous values; ordinary paragraph processing evaluates chapter/page labels even before an empty bookmarks loop.
A level-zero list suffices independently of excessive ilvl iteration; bounding level indices alone does not bound Chicago label length.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): Numbering levels accept an uncapped u32 start and the counter renderer passes it to format_num. The Chicago formatter repeats its selected symbol n/4 times without a label-length budget. Page numbering and the DOCX-to-Markdown list view call the same formatter, so the same missing control affects distinct consumers.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): Numbering start/startOverride values enter u32 counters with only max(1). `Numbering::render()` calls `format_num()`, whose Chicago branch repeats one marker `(n-1)/4+1` times without an output budget.

previousFindings.summary: An untrusted DOCX can select Chicago numbering with a huge list start/startOverride or section page start. The shared chicago_label formatter repeats a UTF-8 symbol roughly n/4 times without a length bound, allowing gigabyte allocations during list rendering, ordinary section-page processing and Markdown numbered-list views. Authored endnote starts also reach this shared formatter. The supplied u32::MAX framing selects 1073741824 double-daggers, about 3 GiB of UTF-8 label bytes; this is static arithmetic.

validation.summary:
The validated traces establish full-u32 list/startOverride propagation and independent section-page and Markdown numbered-list callers. A level with chicago, lvlText %1 and start 4294967295 yields 1073741824 repetitions of a three-byte symbol, requesting 3 GiB before shaping/copying. Section labels are evaluated on ordinary paragraphs even without bookmarks. Alphabetic/Roman siblings cycle at explicit maxima; Chicago does not. Source XML remains small and shallow.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Independently traced DOCX w:lvl/w:start -> NumLevel.start -> next_marker/render -> format_num(Chicago) -> chicago_label::repeat; Markdown list labels call the shared list_number formatter.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): For n=4294967295, chicago_label computes i=4294967294 and repeats the three-byte double-dagger symbol 1073741824 times, requesting 3221225472 bytes before additional copies. A normal numbered paragraph with numFmt=chicago and lvlText=%1 reaches the list renderer. pgNumType/@start with fmt=chicago reaches the page-label branch, and Markdown list_marker delegates to list_number. ZIP/XML depth/byte bounds do not constrain the numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Verified initial counter selection, render formatting and repeat arithmetic. A start of 4294967295 selects the double-dagger marker and requests 3,221,225,472 UTF-8 bytes. XML size and depth remain small; source byte limits cannot prevent the allocation.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): For n=2147483647, i=n-1=2147483646; i%4=2 selects the three-byte double dagger, and i/4+1=536870912 produces 1610612736 bytes before copies. List starts, startOverride, reader starts, endnote numStart and page pgNumType.start are parsed without a maximum. Both Numbering::render and the agent reader call the shared formatter. The native read_view adapter calls markdown::read (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:899-901).
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Parent verified all reported callers of format_num/chicago_label. Rendering list and startOverride, page numbering and endnote numbering accept attacker u32 values; Markdown passes parsed starts/overrides to the same formatter. This is distinct from oversized list-level iteration: even ordinary level zero reaches it.

reachability.outcome: Memory/CPU exhaustion and process termination or WASM failure
preconditions: Victim invokes document rendering on the supplied file.
Victim renders a document containing the supplied chunk.
Victim renders attacker-supplied DOCX containing an internal HTML/MHT altChunk.
reachability.summary:
Default public PDF/PNG converter expands internal altChunk parts after admission. Attacker needs only control over a document processed by the victim.
Untrusted document suppliers reach this importer whenever the public renderer processes their DOCX. The input need not be large, and no release/OS authority is needed.
Public Rust PDF/render APIs and Python/WASM wrappers accept document bytes. A normal table in an internal HTML altChunk reaches this path after admission; no special host setting or raised input limits are required.

attackPath.summary:
Have a victim render a DOCX whose internal HTML/MHT altChunk contains
x
, or another excessive positive span. The generator expands effective columns before the main DOM and later table-vector controls. Provide a small internal HTML altChunk with a single table cell using an oversized colspan, then convert the containing DOCX to PDF/PNG or request its layout.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.
Supplied discovery-0030 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Verified that `with_layout` admits the package then calls `altchunk::expand`, whose HTML cell parser forwards an unrestricted positive usize to the grid-writing loop. A single table/cell with colspan=1000000000 needs no arithmetic overflow to force huge output.

dataflow.outcome: Unbounded intermediate markup exhausts CPU/memory.
dataflow.summary:
DOCX altChunk relationship -> package bytes -> chunk_html -> html_to_wml -> arbitrary usize cell span -> sum cols -> gridCol append loop -> memory/CPU exhaustion
DOCX bytes → with_layout admission → altChunk relationship load → HTML td colspan → cell span → end_table cols → per-column String growth.
Attacker supplies DOCX main XML containing w:altChunk with an internal relationship to an HTML/MHT part -> with_layout -> altchunk::expand -> html_to_wml -> Builder::start parses td/th colspan -> Builder::end_table sums spans -> billion-iteration String generation before DOM parse.

additionalSourceStatements: Excess CPU work and memory allocation can terminate or stall the conversion process.
impact.why:
A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory.
Loss of embedding process/instance availability.

likelihood.why:
No special feature option or external resource is needed; a small valid HTML chunk suffices.
A small numeric HTML field directly determines work.

limitations: No file disclosure or code execution established.

reachability.summary:
Default public PDF/PNG converter expands internal altChunk parts after admission. Attacker needs only control over a document processed by the victim.
Untrusted document suppliers reach this importer whenever the public renderer processes their DOCX. The input need not be large, and no release/OS authority is needed.
Public Rust PDF/render APIs and Python/WASM wrappers accept document bytes. A normal table in an internal HTML altChunk reaches this path after admission; no special host setting or raised input limits are required.

attackPath.summary:
Have a victim render a DOCX whose internal HTML/MHT altChunk contains
x

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.
Supplied discovery-0030 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Verified that `with_layout` admits the package then calls `altchunk::expand`, whose HTML cell parser forwards an unrestricted positive usize to the grid-writing loop. A single table/cell with colspan=1000000000 needs no arithmetic overflow to force huge output.
Supplied discovery-0029 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Confirmed a one-cell table with colspan=1000000000 selects a billion-iteration serialization loop, even though the source table is only dozens of bytes. The check occurs after source admission and before any generated XML parse. The value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.

reachability.summary:
Default public PDF/PNG converter expands internal altChunk parts after admission. Attacker needs only control over a document processed by the victim.
Untrusted document suppliers reach this importer whenever the public renderer processes their DOCX. The input need not be large, and no release/OS authority is needed.
Public Rust PDF/render APIs and Python/WASM wrappers accept document bytes. A normal table in an internal HTML altChunk reaches this path after admission; no special host setting or raised input limits are required.

attackPath.summary:
Have a victim render a DOCX whose internal HTML/MHT altChunk contains
x

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.
Assigned discovery-0031 corroborates colspan=1000000000 causing tens of gigabytes of generated XML and work before layout; rejecting invalid, negative or zero spans does not bound valid positive values.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow. validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.
Supplied discovery-0030 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Verified that `with_layout` admits the package then calls `altchunk::expand`, whose HTML cell parser forwards an unrestricted positive usize to the grid-writing loop. A single table/cell with colspan=1000000000 needs no arithmetic overflow to force huge output.
Supplied discovery-0029 corroboration (already-validated Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Confirmed a one-cell table with colspan=1000000000 selects a billion-iteration serialization loop, even though the source table is only dozens of bytes. The check occurs after source admission and before any generated XML parse. The value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.

impact.why:
A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory.
Loss of embedding process/instance availability.

counterEvidence: Archive admission runs before expansion and limits actual input bytes, not the numeric span or generated XML (src/admission.rs:531-551).
Existing tests handle invalid, negative and zero spans and ordinary span 2, but show no maximum-span rejection (src/convert/altchunk.rs:1026-1054).
SECURITY.md requires hosts to apply process CPU/memory limits; these mitigate host scope but do not bound this loop.
limitations: No application execution or vulnerability-triggering input was used in this static audit.
validation.summary: `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

controls: Malformed, negative and zero spans fall back to one, and tests cover those cases. Positive large integers remain accepted. The generated XML is constructed before DOM parsing or any subsequent processing could reject it.

dataflow.summary: The converter expands package-local altChunks after admission. Builder::start accepts td/th colspan as any positive usize. Builder::end_table sums these values into cols and appends one w:gridCol element for every column without a column or output-size limit.

with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

validation.summary:
Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

finding.summary: Rendering a DOCX with a related HTML table containing `colspan=1000000000` makes the converter append one billion XML grid columns. The input stays tiny and passes archive admission, but PDF, PNG, and layout-report operations can consume excessive CPU and memory or terminate their host process.
finding.title: Rendering an HTML altChunk can exhaust memory through its colspan

counterEvidence: Archive admission runs before expansion and limits actual input bytes, not the numeric span or generated XML (src/admission.rs:531-551).
Existing tests handle invalid, negative and zero spans and ordinary span 2, but show no maximum-span rejection (src/convert/altchunk.rs:1026-1054).
SECURITY.md requires hosts to apply process CPU/memory limits; these mitigate host scope but do not bound this loop.
limitations: No application execution or vulnerability-triggering input was used in this static audit.
validation.summary: `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

controls: Malformed, negative and zero spans fall back to one, and tests cover those cases. Positive large integers remain accepted. The generated XML is constructed before DOM parsing or any subsequent processing could reject it.

dataflow.summary: The converter expands package-local altChunks after admission. Builder::start accepts td/th colspan as any positive usize. Builder::end_table sums these values into cols and appends one w:gridCol element for every column without a column or output-size limit.

rootCause.summary:
with_layout expands document-selected altChunk bytes after original ZIP/XML admission. HTML Builder::start accepts a colspan up to usize::MAX, end_table sums spans and emits gridCol once per declared column. No maximum column count or generated-WML byte budget is passed into expand, so a short HTML table can demand gigabytes before parser/output safeguards can act. The assigned corroborating trace follows Builder::start, end_cell, HTML tokenizer close/end_table dispatch, per-row span summation and the pre-DOM grid-generation loop; page/raster limits occur later.
The HTML importer treats document-supplied colspan as a trusted expansion count. It sums spans and serializes a physical XML column for every claimed slot without checking a maximum or generated byte budget.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `with_layout()` admits the package, then expands its HTML altChunk. `Builder::start()` parses `colspan` into `usize` and only enforces a minimum. `end_table()` uses the span sum as `cols` and appends a grid element once per column without bounding generated output. The XML output loop precedes layout/page raster bounds; rejecting only overflowing sums would leave a single enormous valid machine-integer span reachable.

severity.changeConditions: A strict generated-output and column budget enforced before expansion removes this path; process limits contain its blast radius.
severity.rationale: A tiny attacker-controlled document field causes highly amplified resource consumption in public conversion paths. Impact is processing availability; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

previousFindings.summary: A document author can place a huge positive colspan in a small embedded HTML/MHT altChunk table. Ordinary DOCX rendering generates one grid XML element per effective column after original package admission and before DOM/layout checks. A count of 1000000000 drives a billion appends; 4294967295 generates over 85 GB of markup, exhausting CPU/memory. The supplied positive 4294967295 framing fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and needs no arithmetic overflow.

Parent verified that colspan=1000000000 fits both native and wasm32 usize, survives the minimum-one conversion and drives one billion String append iterations. The original HTML stays small and normal input admission does not inspect its numeric semantics or charge generated XML.
The newly assigned source supplies the larger positive usize framing colspan=4294967295 and derives over 85 GB of grid-column markup. The supplied candidate gave an approximate ~90 GB estimate; these are approximate source-derived output sizes, not runtime measurements. The same generator is reached with HTML or MHT and must be stopped before main DOM parsing.
Verified that even one cell in one small HTML chunk reaches the unrestricted span parser and that closing the table generates a grid sized by the span. A billion-column positive value fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and implies tens of gigabytes of grid markup without needing integer overflow.
Static trace confirms render/docx_to_pdf enter with_layout, admit the original package, load the internal chunk, parse an arbitrary usize span, and loop cols times in end_table. No schema validator or semantic span limit intervenes; a one-billion-column span fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize.
Assigned discovery-0008 corroboration: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Public PDF and render-report APIs reach `with_layout()`, which expands HTML from a local package relationship. A one-cell table with a very large valid `colspan` reaches `0..cols` before DOM/layout checks. ZIP byte, entry, and XML-depth budgets cannot bound this numeric expansion.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): `with_layout` resolves a related package part and invokes `expand`; `expand` routes HTML/MHT to `html_to_wml`. The tokenizer dispatches a `td` to `Builder::start`, whose positive usize span has no upper bound. Closing `table` invokes `end_table`, which writes one record per span before parsing the resulting XML. `1000000000` fits both 32-bit and 64-bit usize and avoids relying on integer overflow.

rootCause.summary: The nesting guard tracks recursive parser calls. nested_list instead iteratively takes its previous output node as a new script base, preserving existing Scripts nodes through take_base. Writer::node recurses into that unbounded base through argument/nodes; no AST-depth or iterative traversal/destruction control intervenes.

merges.subsumption: Same missing WMF record-local boundary across whole-file reads. corroboratingRootCause.summary: raster_wmf verifies only that each declared size fits in the remaining file. TEXTOUT and EXTTEXTOUT then resolve count-sized strings and coordinates against data, not a slice of that record, and retain owned MetaText. The cursor advances by the small declared size, allowing subsequent records to reinterpret and copy overlapping bytes. POLYGON, POLYPOLYGON and POLYLINE share the same missing record-local boundary.

reduction0023.rationale: Same WMF declared-record extent versus whole-file payload readers and short cursor advance. Retained shared record-limited slices with field/count checks and cumulative text/geometry budgets subsume TEXTOUT, EXTTEXTOUT, POLYGON, POLYPOLYGON and POLYLINE. Preserve nonzero mapping, nonblank text and sufficient trailing coordinates/data prerequisites, bounded canvas and EMF countercontrols, and whole-file memory safety.
reduction0023.remediation: Parse each WMF record exclusively through a slice of its declared extent, validate count-derived payload lengths before allocation, and impose aggregate retained-text and operation budgets.

confidence.rationale: Parent verified image reachability, whole-buffer field reads, owned text retention and short-record advancement in current source; no runtime reproduction.

extensions.semanticReductionNotes:
The supplied static proof framing uses repeated eight-byte WMF polygon records with count 65535. In a roughly 512 KiB file, the first roughly 32768 records can each decode following-record bytes as 65535 points, exceeding two billion decodes plus polygon scans before late truncation refusal. META_POLYGON, META_POLYPOLYGON and META_POLYLINE all need record-local bounds; the 384-pixel canvas cap, whole-file safe reads and bounded EMF helper do not enforce those WMF record bounds.
dedup-0003 merges the same shared WMF record-slice violation, rather than a mere media/sink family match. Preserve both proof tuples and all five handlers: eight-byte polygon records with count 65535 in ~512 KiB yield >2 billion point decodes; 10000 fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records claiming 65535 bytes with sufficient nonblank following data yield 655350000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from ~205.6 KB. Text records need nonblank decoded content and valid ordinary mapping to retain MetaText; EXTTEXTOUT rectangle/options and TEXTOUT padding/coordinate layouts require record-local checks. The text source independently validates its text consequences, while previous validated evidence establishes geometry consequences. Actual failure thresholds remain unmeasured. The common remediation limits the slice at dispatch for every handler; fixing only polygon handlers would not subsume the text source. MAX_SIDE=384, object-count clamps and safe whole-file reads remain useful but do not limit these repeated payloads.
dedup-0005: Same raster_wmf record extent versus whole-file handler access. Mandatory checked record slices across all field/string/font/geometry handlers subsume the assigned text and geometry report; a geometry-only patch would not. The assigned proof uses nonzero placeable bounds, fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT y/x/count/options headers with options=0 and n=65535, no local text, and tens of thousands of records in roughly 1 MB to retain several GB of overlapping decoded strings. This supplements, rather than replaces, the prior 10,000-record/~205.6 KB text and ~512 KiB polygon proofs. rootCause.summary: raster_wmf checks declared size*2 against remaining file bytes but keeps passing the entire data slice to its handlers, then advances only by the declared record size. Polygon, polypolygon and polyline counts therefore cause coordinate reads/allocation/raster work across later records. validation.summary:
Parent independently read raster_wmf dispatch/record checks and all three polygon handlers, their file-wide reads and outer offset increment. Repeated eight-byte polygon records with point-count 65535 can repeatedly consume later record bytes as coordinate payload; a 512KiB file supports more than two billion decodes before a late truncation refusal. This is bounded by whole-file bytes rather than record bytes; no memory out-of-bounds access is claimed.
Verified that text counts are u16, checked against the entire buffer, and do not need to fit the declared record. A 14-byte EXTTEXTOUT record can claim 65,535 text bytes beyond its own end. Ten thousand such records with enough trailing bytes imply 655,350,000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from about 205.6 KB of WMF; UTF-8 conversion and later text handling can add cost.
Additional static proof: a placeable WMF with nonzero mapping bounds and fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records (y/x/count/options, options zero, n=65535, no record-local text) reads following records into retained strings. Tens of thousands of such records in roughly 1 MB imply several GB of overlapping decoded text. This is an estimate from the supplied source, not executed memory measurement; ordinary bounds, nonblank content and sufficient trailing data are prerequisites.

extensions.semanticReductionNotes:
The supplied static proof framing uses repeated eight-byte WMF polygon records with count 65535. In a roughly 512 KiB file, the first roughly 32768 records can each decode following-record bytes as 65535 points, exceeding two billion decodes plus polygon scans before late truncation refusal. META_POLYGON, META_POLYPOLYGON and META_POLYLINE all need record-local bounds; the 384-pixel canvas cap, whole-file safe reads and bounded EMF helper do not enforce those WMF record bounds.
dedup-0003 merges the same shared WMF record-slice violation, rather than a mere media/sink family match. Preserve both proof tuples and all five handlers: eight-byte polygon records with count 65535 in ~512 KiB yield >2 billion point decodes; 10000 fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT records claiming 65535 bytes with sufficient nonblank following data yield 655350000 source bytes decoded into retained Strings from ~205.6 KB. Text records need nonblank decoded content and valid ordinary mapping to retain MetaText; EXTTEXTOUT rectangle/options and TEXTOUT padding/coordinate layouts require record-local checks. The text source independently validates its text consequences, while previous validated evidence establishes geometry consequences. Actual failure thresholds remain unmeasured. The common remediation limits the slice at dispatch for every handler; fixing only polygon handlers would not subsume the text source. MAX_SIDE=384, object-count clamps and safe whole-file reads remain useful but do not limit these repeated payloads.

Mandatory checked record slices across all field/string/font/geometry handlers subsume the assigned text and geometry report; a geometry-only patch would not. The assigned proof uses nonzero placeable bounds, fourteen-byte EXTTEXTOUT y/x/count/options headers with options=0 and n=65535, no local text, and tens of thousands of records in roughly 1 MB to retain several GB of overlapping decoded strings. This supplements, rather than replaces, the prior 10,000-record/~205.6 KB text and ~512 KiB polygon proofs.
