rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.

rootCause.summary: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.
Assigned discovery-0031 corroborates both established decoders independently: ordinary HTML/MHT paragraph text reaches the HTML helper even when script/style content is skipped, while an internal fontTable target reaches redundant XML decoding before any absent-part lookup. Its supplied offline dependency evidence identifies oxml-opc 0.14.2 and quick-xml 0.41.0 attribute normalization, independently supported by the repository target round-trip test. No reducer dependency inspection occurred.

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

on:

# Every job only reads the repo; anything not listed here is `none`.
# One run per PR (or branch): a new push cancels the PR's older run, and
# on main a newer commit replaces any run still waiting. The self-hosted
# runners are few, so superseded runs must not hold the queue.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly
codeEvidence.explanation: The coverage job executes the checked-out local action and tests with runner OS authority.
codeEvidence.label: Coverage runs proposed tests on self-hosted runner

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

on:

# Every job only reads the repo; anything not listed here is `none`.
# One run per PR (or branch): a new push cancels the PR's older run, and
# on main a newer commit replaces any run still waiting. The self-hosted
# runners are few, so superseded runs must not hold the queue.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:

test:
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }})
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [self-hosted, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@89b12181fb390509a0842a86cc55eeb8eb928c1d # stable branch, pinned 2026-10-01
      - if: matrix.os == 'self-hosted'
        uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      - if: matrix.os != 'self-hosted'
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6 # v2.9.2
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-nextest
      # Every failing test, not just the first binary's (the `ci` profile
      # does not fail fast), with JUnit XML for Codecov's test results.
      # The strict Markdown round trip is red until the reader work lands
      # (spec 2026-10-13 §5.4); md-roundtrip.yml is its gate, so this job
      # keeps reporting every other test.
      - run: cargo nextest run --all-features --profile ci -E 'not test(markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly)'

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

on:

    branches: [main]

# Every job only reads the repo; anything not listed here is `none`.
# One run per PR (or branch): a new push cancels the PR's older run, and
# on main a newer commit replaces any run still waiting. The self-hosted
# runners are few, so superseded runs must not hold the queue.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

permissions:

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly
codeEvidence.explanation: The coverage job executes the checked-out local action and tests with runner OS authority.
codeEvidence.label: Coverage runs proposed tests on self-hosted runner

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:

          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

previousFindings.remediation: Move untrusted PR jobs to GitHub-hosted or disposable isolated runners with no reusable writable state, credentials or private network. Reserve shared self-hosted runners for trusted protected-branch events and apply the boundary consistently across all affected workflows.
remediationTests: Check that fork/proposal events cannot select the shared self-hosted pool.
Validate trusted branch jobs preserve intended build/cache behavior.

rootCause.summary: The workflows select shared self-hosted runners for pull_request events and execute code from the proposed checkout without a visible trusted-source gate or job-level isolation. A contributor can alter the repository-local composite action or build/test/example scripts. GitHub-token read permissions limit API authority but not the runner account's filesystem and network capabilities.

severity.changeConditions: Verified automatic untrusted-fork execution on persistent unsandboxed shared runners would raise likelihood and severity; disposable isolated runners without shared state/private network would lower or remove impact.
severity.rationale: Compromise of runner-accessible files and private-network authority is high impact. Likelihood is medium because GitHub contributor-approval settings, runner lifecycle/isolation and actual deployment are not visible in the repository. Read-only workflow tokens do not contain the process. No root, release-key or Docker-socket access is claimed.

previousFindings.summary: CI, Markdown roundtrip, Adoption and Docs check out pull-request changes and execute their local actions, build code or scripts on self-hosted runners. A permitted malicious PR run can execute arbitrary shell code as the runner account, with access to source-described shared state and a private cache network.

counterEvidence: GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only and checkout does not persist credentials; neither is an OS sandbox.
GitHub approval settings can prevent individual runs; their current configuration was not queried.
Cache clients say PRs read only; arbitrary proposal code need not use that client, but server write behavior was not inspected and cache poisoning is not claimed.
External runner setup could add isolation absent from workflow source.
limitations: No PR submitted, runner contacted or code executed; infrastructure configuration remains unverified.

validation.summary: CI and Markdown roundtrip accept all pull requests; Adoption and Docs accept relevant path changes. Each selects self-hosted and checks out the proposal before executing local action/build/script content. Additional CI fuzz, package, Python and script jobs share this exposure. The mbx action expressly describes shared private Docker networking, a tokenless HTTP cache, reused checkout state and a shared disk. No fork/actor guard analogous to the Jules workflows is present in these jobs.

dataflow.summary: Pull-request checkout -> local composite action/Cargo/test/bash script -> self-hosted process -> runner files and private-network access

impact.why: Runner-accessible state and private infrastructure can be reached.

likelihood.why: Approval and host-isolation settings are outside visible source.

reachability.outcome: Arbitrary code under runner account authority
preconditions: The PR workflow run is allowed by repository approvals.
Assigned runner retains the shared filesystem/network authority described in source.
reachability.summary: An external contributor needs GitHub to permit the run; they do not need repository merge or runner-administration authority. The source-described shared resources distinguish this from isolated disposable CI execution.

attackPath.summary: Submit a relevant PR modifying a local action, build script or invoked example; if its workflow run is permitted, code executes in the self-hosted job.

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

preventiveControls: Separate untrusted PR compute and trusted push/release infrastructure.
previousFindings.remediation: Run all untrusted pull-request jobs on fresh isolated hosted runners, or enforce disposable self-hosted sandboxes with no trusted shared state, internal service access or reusable credentials. rootCause.summary: The `pull_request` trigger schedules the checked-out contribution on `self-hosted` without a trusted-origin guard. The local `.github/actions/mbx` action and Cargo/test/script commands run with the runner account and its network access. The private-network restriction described for `mbx-cache` does not distinguish PR code from trusted jobs once both execute on these runners.

severity.changeConditions: Reduce severity if PR jobs are proven to use disposable runners with no shared state or internal network; raise it if persistent credentials or a writable cache consumed by trusted builds are confirmed.
severity.rationale: The boundary crosses from a fork contribution into the internal runner environment. The attacker can execute arbitrary job code and contact the documented private cache; persistence, cache poisoning and access to other services depend on deployment details not established by source. GitHub approval settings may require a maintainer to permit the run.

previousFindings.summary: A contributor whose pull-request workflow is permitted can execute modified build/test or local-action code on the project's self-hosted runners, gaining their internal network and shared local build state. The source explicitly places these runners on a private Docker network with a tokenless shared cache.

counterEvidence: Job tokens have contents:read and checkout persist-credentials:false; neither removes host/network authority from arbitrary job code.

limitations: Runner lifecycle, fork run policy and cache server-side authorization are unavailable in the authorized source.

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
codeEvidence.explanation: A client read-only policy and private-network location are not an isolation boundary for arbitrary runner code. Actual server authorization is unverified.
codeEvidence.label: Private cache trust assumption

codeEvidence.code:
# Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
    - name: bound mbx's disk use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        echo "MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        mbx clean --under "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
        MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB mbx gc
codeEvidence.explanation: Clearing the build target is not complete runner reimaging or separation of other writable persistent state.
codeEvidence.label: Runner state persists across jobs

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
codeEvidence.explanation: Self-hosted private shared cache without token
codeEvidence.label: Self-hosted private shared cache without token

codeEvidence.code:
# Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
    - name: bound mbx's disk use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        echo "MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        mbx clean --under "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
        MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB mbx gc
codeEvidence.explanation: Runner checkout and disk are reused
codeEvidence.label: Runner checkout and disk are reused

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
codeEvidence.explanation: Repository configuration documents a shared private network/cache with no token and configures its endpoint.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache is exposed to those runners

codeEvidence.code:
# Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
    - name: bound mbx's disk use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        echo "MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        mbx clean --under "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
        MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB mbx gc
codeEvidence.explanation: The documented execution environment shares persistent stores/disk; it is not configured as an isolated per-PR job here.
codeEvidence.label: Runner checkout and stores are reused

runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@89b12181fb390509a0842a86cc55eeb8eb928c1d # stable branch, pinned 2026-10-01
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c18668ad3cf93ea998bef934396af7bb5c839dc7 # v10.2.0
      # The generator runs jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs against

        with:
          node-version: "24"
      - name: Regenerate and compare
        run: scripts/gen_docs.sh --check

rootCause.summary: CI admits `pull_request` events without a same-repository/trusted-ref gate for self-hosted jobs. The checkout runs before local composite actions and Cargo commands, so a contributor can modify an action, build script, test or invoked script. validation.summary:
Parent independently read all four workflows and the composite action, verified all PR triggers and affected runner/script selections, and confirmed documented shared resources. No live CI/cache probe was performed.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): CI and Markdown roundtrip accept all pull requests; Adoption and Docs accept relevant path changes. Each selects self-hosted and checks out the proposal before executing local action/build/script content. Additional CI fuzz, package, Python and script jobs share this exposure. The mbx action expressly describes shared private Docker networking, a tokenless HTTP cache, reused checkout state and a shared disk. No fork/actor guard analogous to the Jules workflows is present in these jobs.
Assigned discovery-0020 corroboration: Parent verified unrestricted pull_request events, self-hosted jobs, checkout/local-action/test execution and private/persistent cache declarations across CI, docs, adoption and Markdown workflows. All share the same trust-boundary failure.
Assigned discovery-0032 corroboration (supplied already-validated Standard assessment; no reducer verification): Verified `pull_request` trigger, `runs-on: self-hosted`, ordinary checkout, checkout-local action and Cargo execution in CI. Verified sibling docs/roundtrip/adoption placement and commands. The mbx composite action explicitly configures http://mbx-cache:7543 and documents a shared private network, no token, reused checkout and persistent stores. Thus permitted PR code runs with that environment's account/network authority under the documented pool configuration.

attackPath.summary: Supply N digits followed by N periods in ordinary unformatted paragraph or table-cell text and induce legacy conversion.

codeEvidence.explanation: Public doc_to_markdown/doc_to_docx convert parsed spans/cells with escape_line. The outer character loop recomputes whether the entire prefix is ASCII digits at every '.' or ')'. Once one period follows a long numeric prefix, each later period still scans all preceding digits before short-circuiting on that first period, making work quadratic.

rootCause.summary: `render_spans()` passes each line to `escape_line()`. For every '.' or ')' the escaper takes the entire preceding prefix and checks whether all characters are digits, without retaining where that initial digit prefix ended. Even after the first punctuation, every subsequent scan traverses the same N digits before rejecting.

rootCause.summary:
Story::blocks and flush_table preserve per-row cell counts from DOC table marks/properties. push_block then chooses maximum row length and pads every row to it without checking width times row count or generated bytes. rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.
severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.

Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.
severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.

previousFindings.summary: The Python and Node CLIs write plans through a predictable .<plan>.<PID>.partial pathname using nonexclusive truncating writes. A local actor who can create entries in the plan directory can preplace a symlink there and make the victim overwrite another file it can write, before the intended plan replacement.

validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.
severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.

previousFindings.summary: The Python and Node CLIs write plans through a predictable .<plan>.<PID>.partial pathname using nonexclusive truncating writes. validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.

paths. It replaces an output symlink itself, not the link's target. Recording

uses exclusive staging but concurrent read/modify/write recordings remain
last-writer-wins, not a serialized append or compare-and-swap.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.

validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.
Assigned discovery-0024 corroboration (supplied already-validated Standard assessment; no reducer verification): Both writers use the plan basename and process ID without randomness or exclusive creation. A symlink at that temporary name is followed by write_bytes/writeFileSync, modifying an unrelated victim-writable file; the later rename moves the symlink itself into the plan path. Native publication uses exclusive staging and is not affected by these adapter copies.

Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. No code checks the staging object's identity. Preview runs first but does not constrain that file. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.
Assigned discovery-0024 corroboration (supplied already-validated Standard assessment; no reducer verification): Both writers use the plan basename and process ID without randomness or exclusive creation. A symlink at that temporary name is followed by write_bytes/writeFileSync, modifying an unrelated victim-writable file; the later rename moves the symlink itself into the plan path. Native publication uses exclusive staging and is not affected by these adapter copies.

reduction0028.remediation: Use exclusive randomized private staging in the resolved destination directory, write through the newly created descriptor, and atomically replace the plan. rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.

Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.

The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. Native `write_plan` now delegates to secure publication, and a current regression explicitly verifies it does not open the legacy partial symlink.
Assigned discovery-0024 corroboration (supplied already-validated Standard assessment; no reducer verification): Both writers use the plan basename and process ID without randomness or exclusive creation. A symlink at that temporary name is followed by write_bytes/writeFileSync, modifying an unrelated victim-writable file; the later rename moves the symlink itself into the plan path. rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (supplied Standard assessment): The edit/add operation path calls _record after normal plan parsing and document preview. _record resolves the intended final plan but constructs a predictable sibling temporary path using the process ID. Path.write_bytes opens that path with normal truncate/follow semantics rather than exclusive creation or no-follow protection. os.replace happens only after the unintended referent has already been modified.

severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.
severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.

validation.summary:
Verified supported --plan plus operation callers, preview-before-write, and both predictable staging sinks. Preview validates plan semantics, not staging ownership. Precreating .plan.json.<PID>.partial as a symlink to a victim-writable file causes that target to receive recorded JSON before rename; no race after the actual write is needed.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified edit-with-plan recording entrypoints, successful plan preview, non-dry-run branch, partial-name construction and write/rename in both adapters. The write follows an existing symlink before rename, so later replacement cannot undo referent damage.
Assigned discovery-0014 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): The source selects _record whenever --plan and inline operations are present. Successful preview and dry_run=false reach partial.write_bytes with no prior exclusive allocation or symlink check. On a platform/directory permitting symlink following, a preexisting temporary symlink directs that write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI's account. The subsequent replace moves the symlink over the plan path. This does not require modifying the legitimate plan target itself.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Python `partial.write_bytes` and Node `fs.writeFileSync` use default creation/truncation behavior after constructing the same predictable name. The CLI intentionally grants ambient local authority to explicitly requested
paths. It replaces an output symlink itself, not the link's target. Recording
a plan through a symlink retains its documented local behavior: the link stays
in place and its resolved plan file is atomically replaced. Plan recording
uses exclusive staging but concurrent read/modify/write recordings remain
last-writer-wins, not a serialized append or compare-and-swap.
