rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.

Independently traced DOCX altChunk HTML text -> html_to_wml -> Builder::text -> decode_entities -> tail.find(';') per '&'; public xmllinq::unescape_xml_text similarly uses suffix.position for each unrecognized '&'.
Assigned discovery-0010 Standard corroboration (source validation, not reducer verification): Parent verified oxml-opc0.14.2 parse_relationship931-937 decodes Target, its quick-xml normalization semantics, PartFs second decoding, and full-suffix scanning. Repeated & is valid admission input and becomes bare ampersands only upstream; target existence is checked after resolution.
Assigned discovery-0007 corroboration (preserved Standard static validation; no reducer verification): Verified parser222-246 and existing decoding regression test1222-1260; resolve_rel_target677-681; unescape_xml_text764-791; renderer main_rel_part21310-21319 and inspect.related766-776. XML encoded & is valid at admission, so the rejected raw-ampersand hypothesis does not block this post-decoding path. Missing target need not be opened before the work occurs.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration (preserved Standard static assessment, not reducer verification): Verified read_relationships delegates record parsing to oxml-opc 0.14.2; inspected its installed relationship.rs:924-947, where decoded_and_normalized_value produces Target values. PartFs::resolve_rel_target decodes again. The helper iterates each ampersand and scans the entire suffix for a semicolon; a decoded ampersand-only suffix therefore takes quadratic time. Renderer main_rel_part and inspector related invoke this resolver before package-key lookup.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Parent verified read_relationships (opc/mod.rs:222-233), repository once-decoded target assertions (1222-1276), local locked oxml-opc0.14.2 decoded_and_normalized_value (relationship.rs:924-937), second unescape (677-681), and suffix scan (parse.rs:768-786). Font-table relationship selection resolves before part existence lookup, so a missing target suffices. One million valid & refs (~5MB XML) imply~500billion character comparisons.
Assigned discovery-0013 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Confirmed valid escaped Target syntax reaches a once-decoded raw ampersand string, then the second decoder's quadratic scan. Notes/story consumers resolve before checking part existence. Exact oxml-opc 0.14.2 parse_relationship at cached relationship.rs:924-938 decodes Target with quick-xml 0.41 normalized attribute values.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): Reviewed the decoder loop through failed entity handling, which advances by one ampersand then searches the next suffix. HTML part byte limits permit large repeated runs; there is no entity-count/work cap. No runtime timing claim is made.
Assigned discovery-0017 corroboration (already-validated Standard static assessment; no reducer verification): with_layout imports the related HTML chunk and Builder::text calls this decoder. For N ampersands without ';', suffix lengths N,N-1,...,1 are searched. The decoder preserves invalid references instead of refusing them. Archive admission scans XML/.rels policy but treats an HTML part as bounded opaque bytes, so the checked-XML malformed-reference countercontrol does not apply.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: Confirmed oxml-opc0.14.2 src/relationship.rs:925-938 normalizes Target; local opc/mod.rs then unescapes again. Reviewed inspect::related and comparison note resolution, which resolve internal targets before loading parts. Correctly escaped input passes strict XML validation, and the missing target does not short-circuit the expensive resolver.

pub(crate) fn related(&self, kind: &str) -> BTreeSet<String> {
        self.pkg
            .read_rels_for(&self.main)
            .into_iter()
            .flat_map(|rels| &rels.items)
            .filter(|rel| {
                rel.target_mode.as_deref() != Some("External")
                    && rel.rel_type.rsplit('/').next() == Some(kind)
            })
            .map(|rel| self.pkg.resolve_rel_target(&self.main, &rel.target))
            .collect()

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.

previousFindings.summary: HTML altChunk text with bare ampersands and the public XML entity decoder repeatedly search the remaining suffix for ';', yielding quadratic CPU work. A valid admitted .rels Target containing repeated & is normalized upstream and redundantly decoded by PartFs, reaching the same XML sink during rendering, inspection, revision processing or comparison even when the target part does not exist. An additional admitted-main-XML route uses an unquoted value whose first character never reappears: the DOM consumes through EOF and decodes a bare-ampersand comment as an attribute, reaching the same quadratic XML decoder. Ordinary bare-ampersand text is rejected upstream and is not this proof. The same HTML decoder is also reached by Markdown-to-DOCX raw HTML blocks and attribute values; its ten-byte accepted-entity bound is applied after the unbounded search.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.

rootCause.summary: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.

findings.remediation: Scan entities once without revisiting suffixes. In HTML, bound the search to the supported entity-length window before looking for ';'; give XML decoding a monotonic parser or bounded entity grammar. Remove PartFs's redundant relationship decoding when upstream supplies normalized attributes; retain the linear XML-helper repair for its other callers and the separate bounded HTML-helper repair. Preserve canonical literal '&' part names and one-time entity normalization through round trips. Preserve the standalone XML helper's documented permissive output for unsupported or unterminated references while making its work linear. Apply practical relationship-target length/work bounds as defense in depth, preserving exactly one normalization pass and the standalone helper's linear permissive behavior. Align admission/DOM attribute token boundaries or reject unsupported unquoted syntax as defense in depth. Preserve the linear XML decoder fix for this comment-to-attribute route; removing only the redundant relationship decode does not cover it. Apply the bounded HTML helper consistently to Markdown raw-HTML block text and attribute consumers, using UTF-8-safe bounded lookahead and preserving recognized entities, malformed literal retention and multibyte text.

Verify ordinary compatible documents still process under unchanged limits.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.
Assigned discovery-0015 corroboration (supplied validated Standard assessment): `Builder::text()` sends HTML text to `decode_entities()`. For every `&`, the decoder calls `tail.find(';')` on the remaining suffix and only then rejects positions over ten. Repeated ampersands without semicolons therefore cause quadratic scans. The assigned current-tree relationship round-trip assertion corroborates normalized targets independently of dependency-version assumptions, and the established internal story renderer resolves the target before checking whether the selected part exists.
Assigned discovery-0023 corroboration: `read_relationships` loads each record through oxml-opc, whose `parse_relationship` applies `decoded_and_normalized_value` before storing Target. Internal consumers pass that decoded string to `PartFs::resolve_rel_target`, which invokes `unescape_xml_text` again. For N escaped ampersands in source, the second pass sees N literal ampersands and no semicolons. Each failed semicolon search revisits the suffix, then advances by one, yielding N(N-1)/2 comparisons. Attribute count, XML depth and package byte limits do not bound this quadratic work adequately.
Assigned discovery-0022 adds tolerant HTML-style attribute boundaries versus DOM first-character-as-quote parsing: comment ampersands can become one large decoded attribute. This is an additional source path to the retained XML suffix-search root; no relationship resolution is required.
Assigned discovery-0026 corroboration: Markdown html_attribute (src/markdown/write.rs:1350-1357) and html_block_text (1415-1425), including Event::Html, reuse altchunk::decode_entities. Both therefore share the HTML helper's full-suffix search before its length filter; these consumers do not require an XML relationship or ordinary malformed XML text.
Assigned discovery-0031 corroborates both established decoders independently: ordinary HTML/MHT paragraph text reaches the HTML helper even when script/style content is skipped, while an internal fontTable target reaches redundant XML decoding before any absent-part lookup. Its supplied offline dependency evidence identifies oxml-opc 0.14.2 and quick-xml 0.41.0 attribute normalization, independently supported by the repository target round-trip test. No reducer dependency inspection occurred.

# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.

    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx

        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

    name: coverage

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.

codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

# Every job only reads the repo; anything not listed here is `none`.
# One run per PR (or branch): a new push cancels the PR's older run, and

    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [self-hosted, macos-latest, windows-latest]

      - if: matrix.os == 'self-hosted'
        uses: ./.github/actions/mbx

        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6 # v2.9.2
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-nextest
      # Every failing test, not just the first binary's (the `ci` profile
      # does not fail fast), with JUnit XML for Codecov's test results.
      # The strict Markdown round trip is red until the reader work lands
      # (spec 2026-10-13 §5.4); md-roundtrip.yml is its gate, so this job
      # keeps reporting every other test.
      - run: cargo nextest run --all-features --profile ci -E 'not test(markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly)'

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-llvm-cov

      - name: Generate coverage (lcov)
        # Run every test, including doctests. Only cfg(test) implementation
        # is excluded from instrumentation; all production code is counted.
        run: cargo llvm-cov --all-features --workspace --branch --doctests --lcov --output-path lcov.info -- --skip markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly

on:

# Every job only reads the repo; anything not listed here is `none`.
# One run per PR (or branch): a new push cancels the PR's older run, and

coverage:
    name: coverage
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@7e38f4b43b4db5c8dd498af069a4f6196df1d067 # master branch, pinned 2026-10-01

          toolchain: nightly
          # Branch instrumentation and doctest coverage require nightly.
          # Production remains supported by the separate stable/MSRV jobs.
          components: llvm-tools-preview
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      # Downloads a prebuilt binary instead of `cargo install` (minutes → seconds).
      # install-action picks the tool from the ref (`@cargo-llvm-cov`) or, as
      # here with the ref pinned to a commit SHA, from the `tool` input.

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: Source describes the runners' shared private Docker network, unauthenticated HTTP cache and reused checkout/disk state; it does not prove a cache-poisoning protocol.
codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and runner state

# Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
    - name: bound mbx's disk use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        echo "MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        mbx clean --under "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
        MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB mbx gc

codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
codeEvidence.explanation: The shared action documents private Docker-network cache connectivity and no client token, extending runner execution beyond an isolated public build worker.
codeEvidence.label: Self-hosted private shared cache without token

codeEvidence.code:
# Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
    - name: bound mbx's disk use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        echo "MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
        mbx clean --under "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
        MBX_GC_MAX_TOTAL_SIZE=20GiB mbx gc
codeEvidence.explanation: The action documents reused checkouts and shared disk/cache state; actual lifecycle/isolation and server authorization remain deployment prerequisites.
codeEvidence.label: Runner checkout and disk are reused

rootCause.summary: Markdown image destinations are decoded into `Drawing` objects and stored by `picture()`. `package::assemble` routes them through `PartRelate::drawing()` to `materialize()`. The dependency graph is attacker-defined flat JSON; `dep_part()` bounds only each index and uses a name set for collision avoidance. It has neither an active-index set nor a traversal budget, so an in-range self edge or mutual cycle never returns.

severity.changeConditions: Process isolation and strict CPU/memory budgets constrain impact; an exposed shared conversion service increases operational impact.
severity.rationale: A compact input deterministically reaches unbounded recursion in a public conversion API. Impact is availability of the processing host; shared-service exposure depends on the caller deployment.

findings.summary: An attacker-supplied Markdown image with a `drawing:` payload can encode a dependency pointing back to itself. `markdown_to_docx` accepts the flat JSON graph and recursively materializes it without cycle detection, exhausting the stack or memory before conversion returns.

counterEvidence: Bounds checks reject out-of-range dependency indexes, but do not reject valid cyclic indexes.

limitations: No application code or vulnerability-triggering input was executed.
validation.summary: Confirmed public `markdown_to_docx` -> `read` -> `picture` -> `package::assemble` -> `PartRelate::drawing` -> `materialize` -> `dep_part`. A drawing with simple valid XML, no boxes, a root relation to dependency 0 and dependency 0 referring to itself bypasses box checks and repeatedly enters the same function.

rootCause.summary: Admission's `is_xml` decision recognizes only `.xml` and `.rels`; an extension-independent exception covers only the main part. Its recursive element parser has no local depth budget.

findings.remediation: Use exclusive unpredictable private staging and hold directory/file handles until atomic publication. Reuse native publication for Python and implement equivalent exclusive/no-follow staging for Node; never reopen an attacker-controlled temporary pathname.

Verify valid and refused recordings, dry-run, cleanup and atomic replacement with a deterministic fake publication backend in unit tests.

rootCause.summary: The wrappers use PID-derived ambient temporary names with ordinary truncating opens rather than exclusive, private handle-based staging.

severity.changeConditions: Use in a shared attacker-writable directory under a more privileged user increases exposure; private directories remove the stated prerequisite.
severity.rationale: Arbitrary file integrity impact requires another local actor with write access to the selected plan directory and knowledge or guessing of the PID; this is a constrained, low-likelihood path.

findings.summary: Both command adapters write plan JSON through a predictable .<plan-name>.<pid>.partial pathname without exclusive creation or link refusal. A local directory writer can preplace a symlink and cause an unrelated file writable by the CLI process to be truncated before the final rename.

limitations: No local filesystem attack was executed.
validation.summary: Validated Node runEdit --plan plus operation flags -> recordPlan and Python _record. Both preview before writing, then open a predictable partial with default link-following behavior. The later rename moves a directory entry and does not reverse the earlier victim-file write.

attackPath.summary: A local attacker plants the expected .<plan>.<pid>.partial symlink in a shared writable directory. The victim records a valid edit/add plan there; the CLI truncates the symlink target with JSON using the victim's file permissions.

findings.remediation: Use exclusive unpredictable staging in the destination directory, retain the opened handle for writing, and rename only that owned regular file. Reuse the native publication implementation for Python where possible; use exclusive creation (wx) with equivalent symlink/race protection in Node.
remediationTests: In integration tests, preplant the historical predictable partial path as a symlink and verify its referent remains unchanged.

rootCause.summary: The host wrappers protect plan validity by previewing the edit, but then create a sibling staging path solely from the plan basename and PID. Ordinary write_bytes/writeFileSync opens an attacker-precreated symlink and truncates its referent. The subsequent rename cannot undo that write.

severity.changeConditions: A demonstrated privileged invocation in an attacker-writable directory would increase impact; exclusive no-follow staging removes the path.
severity.rationale: Arbitrary victim-writable file corruption is security-relevant, but exploitation requires a hostile shared plan directory and predicting or observing the process ID. No remote or privileged deployment is established.

findings.summary: The Python and npm CLIs record edit/add plans through a predictable .<plan>.<pid>.partial file opened with ordinary truncating writes. A local attacker who can create entries in that directory can preplant the staging name as a symlink, causing valid plan JSON to overwrite another file writable by the victim before the rename.
findings.title: Recording a plan in a shared directory can overwrite a symlink target

limitations: No runtime reproduction was performed.
Actual deployment and directory permissions are unknown; a private plan directory prevents this attacker prerequisite.
validation.summary: Parent inspected Python _run_edit/_record and npm recordPlan: successful preview and a non-dry-run lead directly to the predictable staging write, without an exclusive-create/no-follow guard. realpath protects neither staging entry. The Rust publication alternative does not intercept these host writes.

rootCause.summary: with_layout admits the original ZIP, then expands internal HTML chunks. findings.summary: An attacker-controlled HTML table colspan inside a DOCX altChunk is parsed as an unrestricted usize and expanded into one generated WML gridCol per column. A short decimal span can force billions of XML tags before rendering, bypassing admission limits on the original package.

findings.remediation: Validate gridSpan and row gridBefore/gridAfter counts against a bounded aggregate table-column budget before any arithmetic, iteration or allocation. Use checked addition and fallible allocations with typed conversion errors.

rootCause.summary: The table parser interprets declared logical column spans as allocation counts, imposes only a minimum of one, and sums them without a table-width budget. table_block expands cols to occupancy and resolve_table_merges expands open to col+span. InputLimits bounds physical package/XML size rather than these numeric logical counts.

severity.changeConditions: Process resource limits contain collateral impact; bounded table counts and checked allocation remove this amplification.
severity.rationale: Attacker-authored documents cause severe processing-process availability loss through tiny numeric inputs. Public library/parser reachability is established; no remote-service exposure is assumed.

findings.summary: The renderer accepts w:gridSpan and row grid skip values as unbounded usize counts. table_block sizes its column vectors from the summed spans, so a small admitted DOCX can request multi-gigabyte allocations or a capacity-overflow abort in PDF/PNG/report conversion.
findings.title: Rendering a small DOCX table can allocate billions of columns

limitations: No exploit input or application code was executed.
Allocation failure behavior depends on platform and process limits.
validation.summary: Parent verified render -> with_layout admission -> table_block, cell_span and both vector growth sinks. A one-cell table with a representable very large span fits all physical input budgets and forces the allocations. The HTML expansion finding is separate because it consumes resources before this WML parser.
